title: Bad Genius (2017)

lines.narration: A wrench in his hand, and behind his back three boys close on a classmate. He keeps working.
They pin the boy to a roller door, haul his shirt up and mark his stomach.
In the student lot a blonde asks if his beat-up muscle car delivers pizzas. It's not the ride, he says, it's the rider.
Her boyfriend, the jock in thirteen, brags his grandmother could smoke that heap. The teenager recites the Viper's specs back - anyone can read a brochure.
He only races for pink slips. The jock won't bet eighty thousand dollars of car against a heap.
The girl settles it from the edge of the crowd. The winner gets her.
They line up in a half-built housing tract and tear away down the dirt street.
Losing on pavement, he quits the road and cuts straight across the raw dirt lots while the Viper stays on it.
The muscle car tips onto two wheels and leans on the convertible, close enough to touch.
The crowd scatters as the muscle car launches off the dirt and goes end over end.
It settles upside down, wheels still turning, and he hangs in the belt, face opened up.
At the station a detective plays him a bystander's video of the race. He asks for a copy.
Ken and Barbie walk free; their parents are hooked up. Screw-ups like him are a guaranteed conviction, and his car is already crushed.
His mother arrives swinging at him, demanding to know what he was thinking. He stops answering.
Two priors for reckless driving make this strike three. They'll put him away unless someone finds another way.
In the corridor he asks where they are moving this time. Nowhere, she says.
He flies out alone, wedged into an airline seat between strangers.
A cab carries him into Tokyo at night; the city arrives as his own reflection.
Down a lantern-lit alley, his father opens a sliding door - greying, in a dark robe. He expected him tomorrow; Japan runs a day ahead.
He steps back for a coat. A young Japanese woman comes out behind him, takes it and slips past into the alley.
Inside, the flat is one room. He calls the boy Sean and says he meant to be at the airport.
Sean asks where he sleeps. His mother had no other choice, his father says: it was this or juvenile hall.
The rules came from both of them: school, straight back here, nowhere near a car. His bed is a coat alcove.
Before he leaves, his father sets out an alarm clock, a black school uniform, and a note pinned to it.
A wall of ticket machines stops him cold. He ends up on the wrong train, bag trapped outside the door.
Boswell, he tells the teacher, and the class turns to stare at his street shoes. He has never heard of uwabaki.

claim.subject: the American student

lines.narration: At lunch a student in a white headwrap gives his name as Twinkie and tries to sell him a laptop.

claim.subject: the student in the white headwrap

lines.narration: Then he spots a racing wheel by the trays, asks what Twinkie drives, and tells him to show it.
Off the lift comes a minivan painted Hulk green, a monster toy at the wheel.
The van rolls into an underground garage packed with cars and people, and Sean's mouth opens.
He follows Neela, the girl from his class, to a teal car and tells her she wouldn't have that problem with a V8.

claim.subject: the young American driver

lines.narration: DK works the meet in black leather, rising out of a ring of women, his crew collecting cash and phones. The garage is his.
He pulls her cheek to cheek, calls Sean gaijin, and tells him this is not his scene.
Sean doesn't move. He thought a girl could talk to whoever she wants.
She cuts across both of them and tells Sean to go.
Twinkie names the spiky-haired man pawing at her: Yakuza. Mafia.

claim.subject: the friend in the red beanie

lines.narration: Sean calls him out anyway. Nose to nose, he says it first: let's race.

claim.subject: the American in the grey tee

lines.narration: The crowd jeers that he has nothing to race with. Han offers his own car.

claim.subject: the blond-dyed man in the leather jacket

lines.narration: In the lift down, Twinkie spells out what DK stands for. Not Donkey Kong. Drift King.

claim.subject: the friend in the red beanie

lines.narration: He drops into the borrowed car and lets a thirty-second crash course run at his window.
DK pulls Neela into him and holds her there. Sean watches from the driver's seat.
Tyres haze and the two cars break away together, running off down an emptier deck.
Spectators scatter off the wall. Sean's grin turns to a wince as he grinds the borrowed car down the concrete.
DK bursts out onto the neon street in one long drift, and the crowd behind the barriers comes apart.
The battered orange car slides out last and stops, smoking, in front of everyone.
Han stoops to the window as the crowd closes over him.
He edges in through the sliding door long after midnight. His father is sitting up alone in the dark.
On his feet in the lamplight, he asks straight out whether Sean has been racing.
Cornered in the back room, he gets the arithmetic: nowhere else to go, jail if this fails, house rules or out.
He gives the only answer left - yes, sir - and backs off, leaving his father watching an empty doorway.
School lets out. Han is parked across the road, leaning on the wrecked orange car.
Sean promises to get the money. Han asks why he is talking like he has a choice.

claim.subject: the long-haired man in the parka

lines.narration: On the drive the job gets named: a man in a bathhouse owes Han money, and Sean is going in for it.

claim.subject: the long-haired man in the parka

lines.narration: He walks into the bath hall in a towel and stops dead. One enormous tattooed back fills the pool.
He presses anyway. The debtor rises out of the water, wolf inked across his shoulder, and towers over him.
On the night drive the terms land: pick-up, delivery, phone answered at any hour. Sean names his price - teach me to drift.

claim.subject: the long-haired man in the dark jacket

lines.narration: The blond-streaked man at the table does the talking. Sean asks when the next race is.
Cars go up as the stakes - an eighty-six Corolla against a seventy-two Skyline - and the table cracks up.
Then the room changes: business to discuss, and Sean is sent out of it.

claim.subject: the man in the black T-shirt

lines.narration: The gangster in the black tee leans across the table, grinning. By the end Han has dropped his eyes.
At a payphone he tells his father he stayed late at school for extracurricular activities.

claim.subject: the American in the white shirt

lines.narration: Neela has followed him. He tells her to stop - this world is not good enough for her.

claim.subject: the American in the white shirt

lines.narration: She reads him straight back: army brat, moved constantly, parents never home, angry at everything ever since.
Driving home, Han explains the arrangement. DK's uncle takes a piece of everything on his turf. Fifty percent of something beats a hundred percent of nothing.
They argue what a race is even for. Winning only proves you were faster; it should be for something that matters.
Han tells him why: DK's pride is the weak spot - and Sean still owes him a car.

claim.subject: the long-haired man

lines.narration: A patrol car tucks in behind them at a hundred and ninety-seven. Han says those cars top out at one-eighty.

claim.subject: the long-haired man

lines.narration: Han is grabbed and kissed under the mirror ball while Sean stands behind him, part of nothing.
Twinkie steers him off the floor to explain the room: Tokyo's working models, off the clock and bored.
Han hands over the keys to a red Evo. Sean represents him now, not rolling in a Hyundai.
From the yellow coupe Han works the crowd over how bad the drifting is, and they laugh along.
His father is bent into a stripped coupe he found wrecked on the base. It has got potential.
Then, across the engine bay, a Japanese saying: the nail that sticks out gets hammered.

claim.subject: the grey-haired man in the grey henley

lines.narration: On the school roof a ring of uniforms has closed around a blond student and his crew. Sean shoulders in.
Twinkie cuts through the breaking crowd to shout about the business he has just wrecked up here.
Across the roof Neela tells him saving the day is not easy - and that he did all right.
High above the crossing, Sean asks how Han ended up here. Old westerns, Han says - cowboys always ran for the border. This is his Mexico.
Sean asks why Han handed him a car he knew would be wrecked. A fair price, Han says, for knowing what a man is made of.
Sean asks what happens if he refuses. Life is simple, Han says - you make your choices and don't look back.
Over the glittering sprawl: if Han does not drift to win, what does he drift for? Come and find out.
Two cars run the empty boulevard. Through the window the women are laughing, and Han's grin widens. This is what he drifts for.
Daylight on the mountain hairpins. Out here you drift by feeling, the pink-hoodie friend tells him. So feel it.

claim.subject: the friend in the pink hoodie

lines.narration: Shredded tyres cost money, so they work the shopping crowds - Twinkie reckons he could sell rubbers to a monk.

claim.subject: the young man in the red beanie

lines.narration: Across town, the greying naval officer parts the coats of an empty flat. The bed has not been slept in; Sean never came home.
At the garage rail, one of Han's crew in a satin dress tells him he has a visitor, waiting by a car below.

claim.subject: the woman in the satin dress

lines.narration: Han and Sean run the mountain road door to door, and by the last bends Sean is alongside, hands loose.
Under the overpass they eat vending-machine food out of a box, and her guard finally drops into laughter.
Her mother died when she was ten - an Australian who worked a hostess bar. DK's grandmother took her in.
Sean trades his own: parents split at three, then town after town because of him. He made himself an outsider; inside or outside, it stopped mattering.
She drives him up the mountain. Before they could drive, she says, they cut class and snuck up here to watch the older kids drift.

claim.subject: the dark-haired young woman

lines.narration: No past, no future, no problems - just a moment. Then he stops talking and watches her instead.

claim.subject: the young man with short brown hair

lines.narration: Daylight at the dockside yard. Sean wants another set of tyres - his third today, and rubber is not cheap.
A heavyset man in a tank top crosses the lot, Han and the rest behind him. One swing without warning puts Sean face-down.
Blood at his mouth, Neela at his shoulder. He did not just play with fire, a hooded crewman says - he soaked the matches in gasoline.
Still in uniform, she stops in the doorway of a dim club. DK sits with a boot on the table between two hostesses.
She tells him to his face that he has changed. DK smirks, then comes up out of the chair.
He stands over her: her mother was the best trick in Kabukicho. Leave my mother out of this, she says, not stepping back.
He backs her against the wall. Just like her mother, he says - anything for a buck. Would anyone look twice without her uncle?
He keeps talking low into her face until she stops answering. A tear runs down her cheek.
Neela walks into the garage in tears. Sean searches her face and neither of them says a word.
Across the city Kamata comes down a yellow corridor in a white suit and panama hat, and DK greets him as his uncle.
Kamata thanks him for last week and asks about work. DK grins that it is fine and hands across the take.

claim.subject: Kamata

lines.narration: Going through the printouts, Kamata says he cannot understand half of it. DK laughs it off. Then the old man just sits there in silence, and the smile dies.

claim.subject: Kamata

lines.narration: In the blue-lit office DK hears it: his own partner has been stealing from the operation. Han has been taking money out of the books.
Kamata turns the money into a proverb: for want of a nail, for want of a steed, the war was lost.
Kamata comes round the desk, holds out a small framed picture and goes, leaving DK doubled over it.
DK storms into the bay and gets in Han's face about the side deals he has been running. Then he shoves him into the tyre racks.

claim.subject: the man in the black shirt

lines.narration: Han answers evenly: skimming is what they do, what they have always done. The crew only watches from the rail.

claim.subject: the long-haired mechanic

lines.narration: DK pulls a pistol and levels it at his face. Han holds still: without him, DK would still be shaking down tea houses for pocket change.

claim.subject: the long-haired mechanic

lines.narration: Han breaks for his car. Sean and Neela pile into the red Evo, and the cars burst out of the bay.
A dark car comes up alongside and pins Han's coupe into a concrete pillar. A front wheel shears away and he comes off it still driving.
The cars shoulder into a crossing solid with people, nosing bodies aside while Sean and Neela brace against the dash.
The orange car cartwheels past a junction of stopped traffic. Sean stands in the road, staring.
It settles upside down against a kerb. Han is trapped inside and not moving. Neela climbs out of a car nearby.
Sean sprints for the wreck. Before he reaches it the car detonates, and a fireball goes up.
The blast knocks him flat. He gets up. The car burns alone in the avenue with Han inside.
DK stares out at the fire, then rolls past the crowd and accelerates away, leaving Han burning behind him.
Sean is left standing beside the wreck. Han is dead, killed by the partner he built all of this with.
In an empty carriage Sean sits hunched with his head down while Neela stares past him. Neither of them speaks.
In the unlit lane outside the house the two of them turn toward the dark. A shadow moves, and DK walks out of it.
A scuffle in the dark ends with DK's pistol at Sean's head and Sean's father stepping out with a gun levelled back.
Neela argues across the standoff while the pistol stays at Sean's head. He does not move.
Sean's father answers without lowering his arm. By the time it breaks, Neela has gone with DK to get the gun off Sean.
Alone in the alley his father lowers his guard. He says the mess is his to answer for, and his son's wellbeing his responsibility.

claim.subject: the older man in the olive jacket

lines.narration: Sean does not take it. He did this, he has to do this, and he cannot run from it.

claim.subject: the young man in the white shirt

lines.narration: His father presses him to get out of Tokyo. Sean listens, and his face closes over.

claim.subject: the grey-haired man in the olive jacket

lines.narration: He walks away down the dark street without answering, and his father is left watching him go.
Han is in the ground. Sean walks away down the dark street, and his father only watches him go.
In an empty garage Twinkie's answer is to leave town. Sean tells him flat he can't.

claim.subject: the friend in the mint-green shirt

lines.narration: Twinkie tells him the trouble doesn't stop with DK. It runs all the way up to Kamata.

claim.subject: the friend in the mint-green shirt

lines.narration: So Sean says it out loud: DK answers to Kamata, and he intends to talk to Kamata himself.

claim.subject: the young man in the white thermal shirt

lines.narration: He answers quietly, eyes down, and whatever he says kills the argument dead.
Twinkie hauls up his hatch and pries open a hidden compartment.
Out comes a battered leather satchel. Sean counts a thick wad of banknotes; Twinkie says nothing.
Night, steam venting over a crowded street. In dark clothes Sean turns into an alley where men are already waiting.
He walks past gang jackets and a bat as the crowd closes behind him.
At the guarded door he asks for Mr Kamata. A bald elder steps up to size the boy up.
Hands open the bag in the doorway. The elder sees inside and goes still.
The money walks him in, down a dim corridor into a lantern-lit lounge where every head turns.
At a far booth Kamata smokes while an attendant pours. Sean stops at the bar, locked onto him.
DK plants himself nose to nose and they trade words inches apart. Across the lounge, Kamata turns to watch.
A guard holds him off the booth. He lowers his eyes, and the bag goes forward to the table.
The attendant holds the bag open over Kamata. The old man stays behind his cigar and doesn't reach.
He gives the money back and apologises - and names the arrangement out loud: DK is Kamata's nephew.
Kamata shuts his eyes, unmoved. DK throws it back at him - after everything you've done, you're giving me orders.
Nothing from the booth. The defiance collapses, DK's head goes down into a bow, and Kamata answers loudly.
Sean's peaceful solution is a race. He and DK have caused Kamata nothing but problems; let them settle it.
One race, and the loser leaves Tokyo for good. DK barely looks over - he's beaten this kid once already.
Kamata draws on the cigar, weighing it in silence while the boy waits. Then he grants the race.
Daylight. Keep-out tape across the shutter of Han's garage - and the crew come jogging back to it anyway.
Inside, Sean and Neela read an inline-six together, and the shutter goes up.
They shove the striped Mustang in and the build takes it: turbo motor, welders showering sparks.
A Nissan motor in a Ford's bay. Sean breaks loose onto dirt and dusts the hillside turn.
Between runs they meter the engine, and the work carries on into the night with Sean frowning.
Twinkie tells him DK picked this road. It is his mountain, and nobody else has ever reached the bottom.

claim.subject: the young man in the black durag

lines.narration: Hands polish the finished tail - black, twin white stripes, a Japanese plate. The Mustang is whole again.
Then he stands alone at the top, looking down a road that falls away into blue marker lights.
Race night above a floodlit dam. Cars and people line the ledge.
Every head turns one way. Kamata walks in, fedora and overcoat, a minder at each shoulder, the crowd opening for him.
In the Mustang Sean shuts his eyes and breathes himself calm. Taillights climb the unlit mountain.
DK stares flat ahead. Sean glances across once, then locks both hands on the wheel.
A starter in a dark suit throws both arms up between the cars. They drop.
DK smirks through the first bend. The Mustang slides a hairpin of its own.
They run the cliff edge, Sean shouting at the dust as DK pulls clear.
A snap of the shifter brings them level, door to door in orange sparks.
Headlights sweep low. They slide together in smoke, and the Mustang comes out of it ahead.
DK drives into his flank and scrapes him along the edge. The Mustang breaks free.
Door to door down the straight, trading paint, each driver hauling to force the other wide.
Into a guardrail bend DK leans out of his window and drags his car across to crowd Sean off the road.
Sean shoves him wide instead. DK ploughs off the shoulder through the brush, the mountain screams, and Tokyo has a new Drift King.
Inside the losing car the windscreen webs over as it leaves the road and tumbles. Sean runs on alone.
He stops and stares. The crowd sprints the road to swarm his window while the wreck smokes behind them.
Neela reaches him and his strained look breaks into a grin.
Then three men in black come out of the dark. The crowd turns to face Kamata, and Sean's grin dies.
Kamata says his piece straight at him. Sean takes it with his eyes down, and the face behind the cigar sags.
He presses once more, Sean looks past him, and Kamata turns away from the crowd that beat his nephew.
A packed night garage, Twinkie working the crowd for fistfuls of cash as the bets settle.
Neela steps in front of Sean and holds his eye. Twinkie says something, and the smirk is gone.
He leaves the crowd for the driver's seat and rolls out to the line.
His car noses up beside a hulking muscle car, and behind its wheel sits a bald American in a white tee.
They talk across the lane. The sizing-up drops away fast - the challenger laughs, and the new Drift King grins back.
Smoke boils off the tyres, flame spits from the exhaust, and the starter in red throws her arms up.
